On change and impact in organizations, especially as a result of adopting new technologies and tools

By Rafael Monteiro, rafael.monteiro@kukaisolutions.com · November 2026

Also available in: Português · Español

This article was written entirely by Rafael Monteiro. Grammar corrections, typo fixes and fact-checking of quotations were done with the help of a language model (Claude). The translation from the original Portuguese was also done with the help of a language model (Claude).

Introduction

There is a paradox in how companies adopt technology. Ask any manager whether they would like to improve their company's customer service metrics using AI; the answer will certainly be yes. Now ask how many of those same people would like to be served by a robot when they have a personal problem with their phone or their home internet. Usually, few: most prefer to talk to a human.

There has been a lot of discussion about adopting technology in the workplace. There is a constant buzz around artificial intelligence (AI) and how it is going to revolutionize the way we work. A phrase heard again and again in the most varied circles (the media, management, C-level meetings, etc.) is that if you are not adopting some new technology or putting some AI agent to work on something in your company, then you are already behind.

There is a clear risk in the idea that technology — AI in particular — applies uniformly and with obvious benefits to every area; in fact, it does not. AI is certainly the hype of the moment and will bring many changes to the way we work. But it does not apply directly to much of what we already do. What we can say, especially for fields where human interaction is the core (such as Occupational Therapy, Psychology, among others), is the following:

  1. Your business will probably keep running without adopting some of these technologies.
  2. It is even possible that introducing some of them will lower the quality of the service you offer.

Curiously, and even in contrast with these two points, it is also likely that some technology is the solution you need to stop having so many problems in your company, problems that often have nothing to do with the professional's competence:

  • Lack of transparency in spending and costs;
  • Disorganized folders and reports;
  • Irregular, non-standardized documents and processes;

among many other issues, small or large. In general, management and operational problems are abundant in small businesses. Fortunately, many software products already on the market can be of great help.

This text was inspired by the work in Hertzum (2022). My focus, however, is different: its ideas will be adapted to the context of small businesses where human-to-human interaction is the soul of the business. At several points I will be intentionally imprecise: I will use software and tool as synonyms, even though the latter term is broader. Adapt the reading to whatever context makes the most sense for you.

1. A diagram of impact in companies

When we look at the functional structure of a company, we find a good interpretation for the word impact: it can be understood as the propagation of an action from one area (or function) to another (or others), as shown in figure 1.

We can illustrate the concept with a few examples:

  1. "An employee left the company; I hired someone else who does exactly the same thing". There is no impact here at all, since the new employee's work did not change the tasks being performed in any way, did not involve adopting any new technology, and did not even change the way the group works.
  2. "I hired a new manager, who restructured our whole team to meet changes in our customer profile": this is a clear example of impact, where a person is changing a hierarchical structure and workflow.
  3. "We adopted new software that speeds up our work and shortens the time between request and delivery": this is a classic example of technology adoption impacting the way processes are carried out.
  4. "I swapped company A's software for an identical, cheaper one from company B": there will be no direct impact on the company's operations, although the change opens room for secondary impacts (more cash on hand may mean more budget to hire other people, for example).

When we think about a profession whose focus is human-to-human interaction, the possibilities for adopting technology are generally limited to changing processes and operations (case 3 above). So, when you evaluate adopting a new technology, take into account where you want changes and improvements in your operations.

2. The journey of implementing a new technology

Let us make an important distinction right from the start: buying a technology is not the same as adopting it; I understand "adopting" a technology or resource as "using" it. there is an enormous distance between the two.

Integrating a piece of software or a tool into the company's processes can take a long time, or may never happen at all. This adaptation period This is what is called the shakedown period; cf. Hertzum (2022), ch. 1. is also a testing period, in which the pros and cons of adopting it are investigated. Note that this period may or may not coincide with the period in which the tool is purchased. That is because the adoption of a tool often happens in layers — management vs. users — where the former often have perspectives quite different from those of the people who will use the tool day to day. In fact, managers and those who purchase tools generally tend to look at the process through the lens of "macro"-benefits, while end users tend to weigh "micro"-benefits through the lens of extra work, redundancy, adaptation, etc. Clearly, effort and benefit are unevenly distributed across a company's hierarchy. I stress that the cases that interest me most are those in which purchasing decisions are made by the people who will use the tool — as is the case in many psychology and occupational therapy clinics. After this period the company starts operating in a stable way, with the new technology absorbed by its teams and adapted to its processes and operations. However, there are risks along the way, which I discuss next.

2.1. The adaptation period and the risk of failed adoption

The period of adapting to a tool is one of the hardest. During it, conflicts and tensions tend to emerge. Remember, however: this is expected, since both are the raw material of any change whatsoever. It is generally in this phase that the adoption of a tool tends to fail, because the risks are many:

  • Rejection and/or refusal There is an interesting example of refusal to use a technology in the book Creativity, Inc., by Edwin Catmull and Amy Wallace, which tells the story of Pixar, the animation company. In it, Catmull recounts the company's early days, when it was still a division of Lucasfilm (which produced the classic "Star Wars" saga). His team had invented a technology for digital film editing that replaced the hand-crafted technique of handling film reels and "cutting and splicing by hand" that film editors used. To make a long story short: the editors simply refused to use the software Catmull's team had created, which resulted in an enormous failure. ;
  • Discontinued use;
  • Partial adoption.

In my view, the last two are the worst cases, because they may indicate that the software was, from the beginning, incapable of or insufficient for meeting the company's needs. The same outcomes may also point to inconvenience, difficulty of use, or even a lack of adequate training for using it fully.

The path that leads to any of these outcomes goes through a complex cost-benefit assessment made by the end users. Broadly speaking, we can split cost-benefit into factors that promote the adoption of a technology and factors that obstruct it.

Promoting factorsObstructing factors
SpeedPoor fit with the task
ReliabilityLack of support (such as inaccessible IT or no manual)
Ease of useLack of urgency
Accuracy of the toolChange fatigue
FlexibilityLack of participation or engagement from the end-user team

There are three aspects that I see often and that appear in the table above:

  • Lack of urgency: it is not unusual to hear from companies that adopting technology or a new tool is not a priority at the moment. In general, these are companies that suffer from some or many of the following operational and structural problems:
    • Lack of transparency in spending;
    • Lack of transparency in earnings (e.g.: "I don't know how much I earned this month");
    • Lack of internal organization (e.g.: "I don't know which folder I saved the patient's record in");
    • Lack of systematized processes (e.g.: "my employee went on vacation and forgot to write the session report, so I couldn't send it to the health insurer on time", or "my employee needs to send me the picture that's on her phone, but she isn't answering her phone right now");
    • Lack of flexibility (e.g.: "I'm going to travel, but I'll have to take my laptop and my notebooks to see my patients");
    • Lack of security protocols (e.g.: "I keep all my session notes in this notebook, which I lost last week").

    It is very common, especially among administrators or managers of small clinics, to perceive a disconnect between the problems that prevail in the company and the tools that can be used to mitigate them. This is expected, since most of these professionals have little or no training in management, which keeps them from seeing the relationships between an organization's structures, as shown in figure 1; in this case, they tend to see changes as isolated effects, with no impact at all on tasks or on organizational or process structures, and therefore ineffective.

  • Change fatigue: this is the product of very dynamic or unstable environments, where managers are always looking for a silver bullet to boost the company's productivity. In these cases, the end-user team is always testing various tools — usually ineffective ones — to deal with the problems they face day to day. When this happens, every new tool adoption becomes just one more among many, which reduces its effectiveness and worsens the team's lack of engagement.
  • Lack of participation or engagement from the end-user team: it is very common for communication to break down between the party that develops a piece of software and the party that uses it. Many companies run the risk of implementing technologies that, for lack of communication with the end users, fail to meet day-to-day needs. This is a devastating scenario, in which the company bears an unnecessary cost, developers are left in the dark (because they receive no feedback on possible improvements), and users end up operating with suboptimal tools.

Of the three, I find the third terrible, although I feel the first is the worst. Kotter (2008) argues that there are two possible manifestations of the absence of a sense of urgency:

  • complacency;
  • false urgency.

The complacent professional holds the misleading belief that there is no problem in leaving things as they are, since "it has always been this way". False urgency, on the other hand, stems from anxiety to "put the house in order", leading to activities and tasks that produce no results. In my view, this also comes from a huge insecurity in the face of more serious changes and of the need to rethink the workflow in depth, producing a defensive reaction to preserve the status quo. Both, when prevalent, are a very bad sign that it will be hard to get through the adaptation phase and reach the point of reaping rewards at the end of implementing the new system.

3. How to measure the impact of a new tool on your operations

You can be quantitative here and assess how much (in delivery time, or in costs) a change in one area impacted another. Since I imagine this is not very natural for many people, I suggest another path.

One possible approach is to consider qualitatively what kind of gains you are aiming for with the new tool, such as:

  • Better standardization: documents with a more clearly defined structure;
  • Flexibility and security in the custody of patient data: in the cloud, encrypted, accessible only by administrators or by people they have granted access to;
  • Structural organization: data is stored following a fixed logic, not subject to human inconsistencies;
  • Transparency in costs and earnings: simple, practical bookkeeping;
  • Gains in speed: for example, AI transcription can make writing reports faster;

etc. If you lack any of these "virtues" and suffer from not having them, a piece of software that offers them may be useful to you.

4. Conclusion — so, should I adopt a new technology?

Let us start with the easiest cases.

4.1. Some extreme cases — no!

I believe that in the following two cases adopting any software — including Kukai Solutions' own! — is problematic:

  • Extremely "efficient" companies: these are companies that, even without up-to-date tools, manage to operate with a high degree of efficiency and a fully booked schedule. In general, in these cases there is not much room in the schedule to rethink the workflow. Let me be a little more careful here and contrast this with the following observation. There is a great line in the book The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement, by Eliyahu Goldratt, which says that "a plant in which everyone is working all the time is very inefficient". Broadly speaking, the argument is that if there is no room to deal with fluctuations in operations, there will never be the flexibility to meet new demands, and the company can no longer offer new services or serve new customers.
  • Extremely inefficient companies: in this case, especially if there is some gap in professional training, a tool is unlikely to make up for it.

In these cases, at least until other issues are resolved (freeing up room in the schedule or mitigating shortcomings in other areas), I recommend not adopting any technology at all.

4.2. Other cases — probably yes, but think it through

As I said earlier, in section 3, if you can anticipate improvements in operations, elimination of tasks or gains in efficiency, assess:

  • how much time I gained/saved with the change;
  • how much organization I gained with the change;
  • how much flexibility I gained with the change;
  • how much security (of patient information) I gained with the change;

etc. The biggest difficulty in measuring all this is that these are different quantities (money, time, "organization", etc.). You can try to put them into a single unit by using the value of your working hour as a reference, which helps estimate how much this improvement would bring you, and also lets you judge whether the tool is worth its cost.

References

  • Catmull, Edwin, and Amy Wallace. Creativity, Inc. Random House, Incorporated, 2014.
  • Goldratt, Eliyahu, and Jeff Cox. The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement. North River Press, 1984.
  • Hertzum, Morten. Organizational implementation: the design in use of information systems. Springer Nature, 2022.
  • Kotter, John P. A sense of urgency. Harvard Business Press, 2008.

We shall never allow ourselves to drift away intoxicated, in the world of shallow dreams.
